docs.title: Truejoin
docs.text:
One process that opens corporate databases to agents through a reviewed catalog, with row-level security, column masking and an audit trail on every query, whoever wrote the SQL. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle; on-premises, air-gapped if need be.

The console in a minute: console-demo.mp4.

The console in a minute: a tenant's key and an administrator's run the same query, the catalog, a key with row rules checked before it is handed out, and the audit trail.

Claude over MCP: claude-demo.mp4.

The same data read by Claude Code over MCP, replayed as the session ran: one tenant's rows, national ids masked, every read in the audit trail.

It is three projects made into one package: Warp (database to governed REST and OpenAPI, with a catalog a model writes and a person approves), Fusion (in-memory OLAP on DuckDB and the tool surface for agents) and Stargate (OpenAPI to MCP).

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• A REST API per table, with filtering, sorting, pagination, typed schema and streaming export.
  • A catalog: descriptions, semantic types, relationships and business terms, written by a model and read by nothing until a reviewer approves and certifies them.
  • Analytical queries over /olap and MCP: SQL, metrics without SQL, and questions in words. Tables too big to load are read in slices.
  • Follow-up questions. answer_question takes the request an earlier answer returned as previous, and reads "and by branch?", "only the cancelled ones" or "the top 3" as that request changed where the new words say: a breakdown replaces the old one ("and monthly" adds one), a condition replaces one on the same column, an aggregation alone applies to the measure there was. No model, and nothing kept on the server between calls: the caller carries the conversation (the console's Question mode has a box for it). Each column of an answer says what it is (labels: the measure, its aggregation and the catalog's description, or the breakdown and its grain), and the console writes the reading out as a sentence. A question it reads in part lists the words it left out (unread: not in the vocabulary; unused: known, but the reading makes no use of them); one it reads none of, or whose words name tables no one request joins, is answered with SQL a model writes from the schema the caller may see, run under the same guardrails, row rules and masks, and marked as such (olap.unread_questions: sql, the default); with refuse, or with no usable model, it is refused.
  • Governance on every read. A caller's row rules and masks apply to each table a query names, through aliases, joins and subqueries. One audit event per query, never the SQL.
  • Grounding. Joins are checked against the keys the databases declare; query_metrics joins along those keys so a request cannot write a wrong one.
  • Measures from the past. The query history and the views are mined for the definitions people repeat; a reviewer certifies the ones that are right, or writes one by hand.
  • Saved analyses. Questions and the SQL a reviewer certified for them; find_examples hands the closest ones to a model before it writes SQL.
  • Words a reviewer adds. A catalog's abbreviations are written out before a question is matched, and its notes reach a model with the source (list_sources, the OpenAPI x-llm-context). Both are set in the console's Ontology overview or with PATCH /catalog/{db}/guidance, and used once the catalog is approved.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
One hexagonal (ports and adapters) package. Dependencies point inward and one test enforces it: tests/fusion/architecture/test_dependency_rules.py walks every import, lazy ones included.

inbound adapters (HTTP, MCP, CLI, SDK) --> application (services) --> ports (Protocols)
                                                  |                        ^
                                                  v                        | implemented by
                                           domain (pure)        outbound adapters (databases, DuckDB,
                                                                 sqlglot, LLM providers, catalog store)
truejoin.bootstrap wires adapters into the services.
Layer Package May import Domain truejoin.domain.{olap,gateway,governance,catalog,mcp}, truejoin.domain.settings_catalog domain; pydantic for the catalog's file format Ports truejoin.ports domain, ports, truejoin.application.settings; pydantic Application truejoin.application.{olap,gateway,catalog,mcpgen} and its modules (settings, settings_service, access_keys, local_users, databases, usage, container) domain, ports, application; pydantic, structlog Observability truejoin.observability domain, application, observability Outbound adapters truejoin.adapters.outbound.* domain, ports, truejoin.application.settings, their drivers Inbound adapters truejoin.adapters.inbound.{http,rest,mcp,cli,sdk} domain, ports, application, observability, truejoin.bootstrap, truejoin.runtime_mcpgen and their frameworks Composition truejoin.bootstrap, truejoin.main anything

tests/fusion/architecture/test_dependency_rules.py holds the exact rules and checks every import, lazy ones included.

docs.title: One process
docs.text:
truejoin serve runs one ASGI app: the REST gateway (a router per table), the OLAP routes at /olap, and the MCP tools over streamable HTTP at /mcp. The gateway's authentication guards all three: API keys, and bearer tokens from an identity provider, the directory or local users. --transport stdio serves the MCP tools alone. See ADR 10.

The gateway is async (asyncpg, aiomysql, aioodbc) and the OLAP engine is synchronous (DuckDB behind one lock). They meet on a loop thread that owns the OLAP side's database pools; see ADR 11.

docs.title: The path of an analytical query
docs.text:
validate (SELECT only, no file or network functions)
  -> ground (joins against the declared keys: advise or repair)
  -> restrict (each table replaced by the caller's view of it: row rules, masks)
  -> plan (reuse what is loaded, load whole, load a slice, semi-join, or refuse)
  -> execute on DuckDB -> one audit event

Every surface reaches this path: query_data, /olap/query, query_metrics with a join, and answer_question. See ADR 12.

docs.title: The catalog, and who may read it
docs.text:
Analysis writes a draft: descriptions, semantic types, relationships checked against the data, and business terms. A reviewer approves tables; the CLI review, which shows each table's term, certifies it as well. Only an approved catalog labels columns for masking, adds relationships to the join graph, names measures and answers questions. See ADR 13.

Each field a reviewer reads says where it came from. The catalog keeps the model's own text beside the description, name and semantic type (generated_*), who last edited a field and when (edited, beside user_overrides), and, after an analysis runs again, what the model wrote before when it now writes something else (previous_generated). The console shows Model wrote or Edited by …, the edit against the model's text word by word, and what the last analysis changed; setting a field back to the model's text is no edit. Catalogs written before these fields load as they were, with no marks.

docs.title: Configuration: the file and the console
docs.text: A server reads a small YAML file (config/database.yaml) for what it needs before anything else. Everything else is set from the console's Settings tab by an admin, kept in settings.settings_store.path, and served at once: the server rebuilds itself with the new settings before the change is answered. config/reference.yaml lists every setting with comments.

docs.title: What the file holds
docs.text:
These are read from the file only; the console shows them read-only under Startup (file only):

Settings Why they stay in the file settings.api_prefix, mcp.http_path, mcp.stdio_api_key_name Every client's URLs depend on them settings.auth.* (enabled, keys, public paths, OpenID Connect, the directory auth.ldap, local users auth.users) From the console, one mistake or one intruder could lock everyone out settings.audit.enabled, settings.audit.file An intruder must not be able to switch off the trail of what they did settings.masking.hash_secret The pseudonym key: changing it breaks every join on a pseudonym settings.catalog.storage_path, settings.auth.key_store, settings.database_store.*, settings.settings_store.* Where the server keeps what the console changes olap.enabled, olap.database, olap.memory_limit, olap.threads, olap.external_access, olap.temp_directory, olap.max_temp_directory_size The DuckDB engine itself databases The databases every start needs; more can be added from the console (Administration, Databases)

Environment variables stay as they are: APP_ENV, CONFIG_PATH, CORS_ORIGINS (empty means *, which production refuses), API_HOST, API_PORT, API_WORKERS, LOG_LEVEL, LOG_FORMAT; a model's key from OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY when its api_key is empty; the deprecated FUSION_* and WARP_* variables, which still set their olap settings and lock them as the file would; and TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY, the Fernet key that encrypts what the console keeps (database passwords, model API keys) and signs password sign-ins. It is required whenever a store, auth.ldap or auth.users is set: a store without it refuses to start (and truejoin config validate says so), and sessions read it by that name even when a store's key_env names another:

python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())'

docs.title: What the console changes
docs.text:
Every other setting: the API's limits and exports, raw SQL, masking rules, what the audit trail keeps of a question, the catalog and analysis options, the models (settings.llm.*), the languages catalogs are written in, the analytics engine's budgets, cache, rate limit and grounding, remote sources, and the MCP profile and tools.

  • At once. A change is checked as a whole (every validator, and the production rules under APP_ENV=production), kept, and served by a new generation of the server built beside the running one: table routes, /olap, MCP and the catalog. Requests already running finish on the old one, which is closed 30 seconds later. If the new one does not build, nothing changes and the change is not kept. A file-backed olap.database cannot be open twice: then /olap pauses while it rebuilds. A rebuild reconnects the databases and starts the OLAP cache empty; tables load again as they are queried.
  • Locked by the file. A setting the file writes is shown with a file badge and cannot be changed from the console. Delete it from the file to manage it there. A value that reads the environment (${VAR}) stays in the file.
  • Sensitive settings (raw SQL, masking, where samples and questions are sent, sample values in the OpenAPI spec, keeping question text, the models, remote sources, the backup path, the debug routes, the MCP profile and tools) are applied only after their names are typed back.
  • Secrets (*.api_key) are encrypted in the store and never shown; a blank value keeps the one kept.
  • Who. Only a caller with the admin permission (an API key, or a signed-in user whose roles or permissions grant it). With authentication off, changes are refused outside APP_ENV=development.
  • Trail. Each change is an access_change event naming the paths changed (settings olap.cache_ttl,...), never their values.
  • Reset returns a setting to the file's or the default value.
  • Not offered: settings.docs_url, settings.redoc_url, settings.llm.language_prompts, settings.i18n.fallback_language and settings.i18n.auto_translate are not read by anything, so the console leaves them out (/docs and /redoc are served outside production only).
  • Several workers sharing the store pick a change up within 30 seconds.

The same is available over the API: GET, PUT /settings ({"changes": {path: value}, "reset": [path], "confirm": [path]}) under the API prefix.

docs.title: Moving an existing file to the console
docs.text:
truejoin config import -c full.yaml --minimal-out database.yaml

copies every setting the console may hold from full.yaml into the store (the file must name settings.settings_store.path, and TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY must be set), and writes database.yaml with only what must stay: the startup settings, the databases, and any value read from the environment. Serve with the new file. Without --minimal-out it lists what to delete from the file; until then the file keeps those settings locked.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: truejoin is one image, one process and one port. It reads one YAML file and the environment, and it refuses to start in production with an unsafe configuration.

docs.title: What production refuses
docs.text:
With APP_ENV=production (the image's default) startup fails, saying why, when any of these hold:

  • settings.auth.enabled is false;
  • settings.enable_raw_query is true;
  • CORS_ORIGINS contains *;
  • an API key is a placeholder;
  • /openapi.json is in auth.public_paths, unless auth.allow_public_openapi: true accepts that the enriched spec is public. The default public_paths includes it, so a production config sets public_paths: ["/health"];
  • an OIDC issuer or jwks_url is not https://;
  • auth.oidc, auth.ldap or auth.users is set while auth.enabled is false;
  • auth.ldap.url is ldap:// without start_tls: true;
  • auth.ldap or auth.users is set and TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY is not;
  • API keys carry row_filters while auth.enabled is false;
  • a hash mask has a secret shorter than 32 characters (a missing one is refused in every environment).

Always on, in every environment: parameterised queries, mass-assignment protection, timing-safe key checks, masking of personal samples before any model call, and DuckDB's external access latch.

docs.title: The image
docs.text:
make image                     # docker build -t truejoin:dev .

Multi-stage, base images pinned by digest, dependencies exactly as uv.lock names them. The runtime stage has no compiler, no package manager cache and no curl; it runs as uid 1000 and writes only to /app/catalogs, /app/data, /app/logs and /tmp, so it runs with a read-only root filesystem.

Build argument Values DEPS online (default), wheelhouse Where the Python dependencies come from WITH_MSSQL_ODBC 1 (default), vendor, 0 Microsoft ODBC Driver 18: from Microsoft, from docker/vendor/mssql, or none WITH_ORACLE_ODBC 0 (default), 1 Oracle Instant Client from docker/vendor/oracle; never downloaded

PostgreSQL and MySQL need no driver. docker/vendor/README.md says what to put where for the other two.

docs.title: A build with no network
docs.text:
make wheelhouse                # on a connected machine: the locked wheels, ~100 MB
make image-offline             # docker build --network none --build-arg DEPS=wheelhouse

make wheelhouse downloads the wheels inside the builder image, so they match the platform that will install them, and verifies each against the hash in the lock. Carry docker/wheelhouse/, docker/vendor/ and the two base images (by the digests in the Dockerfile) across the gap; make image-offline then fetches nothing. The offline install uses --no-index --require-hashes.

docs.title: Compose
docs.text:
docker-compose.yml is the development stack (the app with reload, PostgreSQL and MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle behind profiles). docker/smoke/ is a production-shaped one: the built image in production mode, read-only, without capabilities, the database password as a mounted file.

make smoke

builds the image, starts that stack and runs scripts/smoke.py against it: twenty-four checks that a tenant reads its own rows over REST, MCP and metrics with the personal column masked and never another tenant's from the cache, that joins follow the declared keys, that a wrong join is repaired, that a question in words is answered, and that each read left one audit event with no SQL in it. It is the release check; run it from a clean checkout.

For Claude Desktop or another stdio client:

docker run --rm -i -v "$PWD/config:/app/config:ro" -e APP_ENV=development \
  truejoin:dev truejoin serve --transport stdio

mcp.stdio_api_key_name says which key's row rules and masks that one caller has.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
helm install truejoin helm/truejoin -f my-values.yaml

The chart runs one replica, replaced on change: the process holds what it loaded and the catalog it started with, so two pods would answer from two copies. values.yaml documents every setting; helm/snapshots/ holds a default and a hardened rendering, which make helm-check compares against.

  • config is the YAML file, rendered into a ConfigMap. Keep secrets out of it.
  • The pod is non-root, read-only, without capabilities or a service-account token; /app/catalogs and /app/data are volumes.
  • networkPolicy.enabled closes everything except what ingressFrom and egressTo name (and DNS): the databases, and the model endpoint if one is used.
  • An approved catalog goes live without a restart: at once for a change made through the API or the console, within 30 seconds for truejoin catalog on the command line. A draft leaves what is live alone.

The chart has been linted and rendered, not installed on a cluster.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Two forms, both resolved when the config is loaded, neither ever logged (truejoin config show masks them):

  • ${NAME} or ${NAME:default}: an environment variable;
  • ${file:/path}: the contents of a file, without the trailing newline. A missing file is an error, not an empty password.

${tenant} and ${username} are not variables: in a row rule they are filled in from each caller, so the loader leaves them as they are.

Prefer files. In Compose they are secrets:; in Kubernetes the chart mounts the keys of secrets.existingSecret under /run/secrets/truejoin.

Vault. truejoin does not talk to Vault and has no SDK for it. Use the Agent Injector: annotate the pod (podAnnotations in the chart) and read what the agent writes with ${file:/vault/secrets/<name>}.

podAnnotations:
  vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject: "true"
  vault.hashicorp.com/role: "truejoin"
  vault.hashicorp.com/agent-inject-secret-db-password: "secret/data/truejoin/db"

masking.hash_secret is a secret like any other: whoever holds it can re-derive every hashed value.

docs.title: Handing out keys from the console
docs.text:
Configured keys change with the configuration file and a restart. With auth.key_store naming a file, a caller with the admin permission can also hand out and revoke keys at run time: the console (Administration, Keys), or GET, POST /keys and DELETE /keys/{id} under the API prefix.

settings:
  auth:
    enabled: true
    key_store: /app/data/keys.json   # on a volume, like the catalogs
    api_keys:
      - {key: "${file:/run/secrets/truejoin/admin-key}", name: admin, permissions: [read, admin]}
  • A key's row rules are checked when it is made: a table or column that no served database (nor an approved catalog) has is refused, with the closest name, since a rule on a misspelt table would restrict nothing and a key cannot be edited. POST /keys/preview (and Check the rules in the console) counts, per table, the rows the rules would leave against the rows you see, before the key exists. It needs the analytics engine; each count is an analytical read audited under your name, plus one event naming the key previewed. Rules written in the configuration file (keys, auth.oidc, auth.ldap) are not checked this way.
  • A new key's secret (truejoin_...) is in the answer that made it and nowhere else; the file keeps its SHA-256 digest, written atomically and readable by the server's user only. Its last four characters are kept as a hint. Each change is made under a lock on <file>.lock beside it, so workers sharing the file never write over each other (no lock on Windows).
  • What it may do is fixed when it is made: permissions, tenant, roles, row rules (as in the config, ${tenant} and ${username} included; checked then), an optional expiry in days. It is never edited: revoke it and hand out another. A revoked key is refused from the next request on, in every process that serves the same file.
  • Nobody gives more than they hold: no permission their own key lacks (all gives any permission), and a caller held to row rules hands out nothing. A new key carries exactly its grantor's roles, in order, all or not: a role can lift masks and row rules, and because a role's own masking rules replace the default ones, a key with a role left off could see more. To hand out keys of another role, give that role an admin key of its own.
  • Names are never reused, a configured key's included, so the audit trail names one key. Handing out and revoking are access_change events (create_key <name>, revoke_key <name>) with who did it.
  • The configured keys are listed beside them, by name and grant only.

docs.title: Adding databases from the console
docs.text:
Databases in databases: change with the configuration file and a restart. With database_store.path naming a file, a caller with the admin permission can also add, change and remove databases while the server runs: the console (Administration, Databases), or GET, POST /databases, POST /databases/test, PUT /databases/{name} and DELETE /databases/{name} under the API prefix.

settings:
  database_store:
    path: /app/data/databases.json  # on a volume, like the catalogs
    key_env: TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY     # the default

# The encryption key, once; keep it with the other secrets.
python -c 'from cryptography.fernet import Fernet; print(Fernet.generate_key().decode())'
  • Passwords. They are encrypted in the file with the Fernet key in TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY. The server will not start with the store set and the key missing. The rest of the file is plain JSON, written atomically and readable by the server's user only. No answer, log line or audit event holds a password; a blank password on a change keeps the one kept. Losing or changing the key makes the stored passwords unreadable: enter them again.
  • At once. A database is connected before it is kept: one that cannot connect is refused with the driver's message (password removed). Once added, its tables are served right away by the table routes ({api_prefix}/{name}/...), SQL (/olap), MCP and the catalog. A change tries the new settings first and, if they fail, the old ones keep serving. Removing takes its routes and its OLAP source down at once; its catalog stays.
  • Names are a SQL schema and a URL segment both: letters, digits and underscores. The names of the server's own routes (catalog, audit, keys, databases, settings, auth) and the configured databases' names are taken.
  • At startup the added databases are connected after the configured ones. One that cannot be reached does not stop the start: it is listed as not connected, with the reason, to be fixed or removed from the console. A configured one still stops it, as before.
  • Who. Every route needs admin. With authentication off, changes are refused outside APP_ENV=development: anyone who reaches the server could otherwise make it connect to any host it can reach.
  • Adding, changing and removing are access_change events (add_database <name>, update_database <name>, remove_database <name>) with who did it, never the host, user or password.
  • Several workers or replicas sharing the file: only the process that made the change serves it at once; the others pick it up on their next start.

docs.title: Signing in with an identity provider
docs.text:
Beside the API keys, truejoin takes bearer tokens from an OpenID Connect provider (Keycloak, Entra ID, Okta, ...). Nobody is stored in truejoin: who a caller is and what they may do come from the token's claims.

settings:
  auth:
    enabled: true
    oidc:
      issuer: https://login.example.com/realms/acme   # as the tokens carry it
      audience: truejoin                                  # aud the tokens must have
      roles_claim: realm_access.roles                 # dotted path; "roles" by default
      tenant_claim: tenant                            # optional
      role_permissions:
        analyst: [read, query]
        steward: [read, query, update, create]
        dpo: [read, query, audit]
      row_filters:                                    # for every caller who signs in...
        orders: [{column: tenant_id, value: "${tenant}"}]
      row_filter_exempt_roles: [dpo]                  # ...but these
      resource_url: https://truejoin.example.com          # this server, as clients reach it

A token is accepted when the provider's published key verifies its signature (RS/PS/ES algorithms only, never none or an HMAC), it names the configured issuer and audience, and it is unexpired (30 seconds of leeway). The keys come from the provider's discovery document and are cached for five minutes; a key id the cache does not know is fetched again, at most once a minute, so a key rotation needs no restart. A token that lacks a claim the row rules need is refused at sign-in. Production refuses an http:// issuer.

The caller's permissions are the union of their roles' (role_permissions) plus default_permissions; masks and the audit trail follow the roles and the name (username_claim, then sub) as they follow an API key's.

MCP clients find the provider themselves: a request without credentials is answered 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata=..., and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource names the issuer (RFC 9728). The client runs the OAuth flow with the provider and comes back with a token; register it there as a client of the truejoin audience.

The console signs its user in when console_client_id is set: Sign in sends them to the provider (Authorization Code with PKCE, S256), and the code they come back with is exchanged by truejoin itself, so the page keeps talking to truejoin only (its CSP is unchanged) and the provider needs no CORS for it. The token is checked like any other before the page gets it, and lives in that tab only. Register the console at the provider as a public client with PKCE, the redirect URI <truejoin's URL>/ui (resource_url when truejoin is behind a proxy), and an access token whose audience is the configured audience (Keycloak: an audience mapper). A token can also be pasted where the API key goes.

When the provider gives a refresh token with the sign-in, the console renews its access token a minute before it expires (and when a sleeping tab is looked at again), through truejoin (POST /ui/sign-in/refresh); the new token is checked like the first, and a rotated refresh token replaces the old one. Both live in that tab's storage only. Keycloak gives one by default; Okta and Auth0 want offline_access in console_scopes. A provider that cannot be reached is a 502, and the console tries again every ten seconds while its token holds. Without a refresh token, or once the provider refuses it (session ended, token revoked), the next call after the token expires answers 401 and the user signs in again.

docs.title: Users made in the console
docs.text:
For a team with no directory, and for the accounts a directory should not hold (a service desk's, a contractor's), administrators can make users in the console (Administration, Users). Name, password and permissions are all it takes; nothing else has to run. These users sign in with a username and password beside the API keys, the directory and the identity provider.

settings:
  auth:
    enabled: true
    users:
      store: ./data/users.json        # password hashes, readable by the server's user only
      min_password_length: 12         # length is what is checked, not which characters
      session_ttl_seconds: 28800      # how long a sign-in lasts
      max_failures: 5                 # wrong passwords per user before sign-in pauses
      lockout_seconds: 300

Someone has to be the first administrator, so the CLI works on the file directly:

truejoin users add yonetici --permission all --display "Yönetici" -c config/database.yaml
truejoin users list | passwd | disable | enable

From then on the console does the rest: make a user, change their permissions, set a new password for them, disable them (a disabled user is refused from the next request on, whatever they were signed in with) or remove them. The same is available over the API under the API prefix, /api/v1/auth/users (GET, POST, PATCH /{name}, POST /{name}/password, DELETE /{name}), all needing the admin permission, plus PUT /api/v1/auth/users/me/password for a user changing their own, which needs only to be signed in and to know the current password.

A name is 1 to 64 letters, digits and . _ @ -. me, admin, root, system and the configured API keys' names are taken, so the audit trail never shows two callers under one name.

Passwords are kept as scrypt hashes (salted, 32 MiB and about 60 ms a check), never in a file, a log, an answer or the audit trail. A name that does not exist costs a hash too, so how long a refusal takes does not say which names exist. A wrong password, an unknown name and a disabled account all read Wrong username or password, and repeated failures pause the name (and, ten times looser, the address) with 429 and Retry-After.

Who may change whom follows the rule for keys. Nobody gives a user more than they hold; nobody held to row rules makes users (a user without them would see what the maker cannot); a user carries exactly its maker's roles (a role can lift masks and row rules, and leaving one off can loosen them); and nobody changes, resets or removes an account stronger than their own, since resetting a password is taking the account over. Nobody removes or disables the account they are using, or lowers its permissions, so an administrator cannot lock themselves out.

Sessions are the tokens of directory sign-in (below). A local user's token carries the name and a fingerprint of the password it was made with, not the permissions: disabling or removing the user, changing what they may do, or changing their password applies to a sign-in already made, at once. Changing a password ends every sign-in made with the old one, the person's own included.

Every change is an access_change event naming the user (create_user ayse, update_user ayse permissions, reset_password ayse, delete_user ayse), never a password. Production needs TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY (sessions would end at every restart otherwise) and auth.enabled: true. A name that exists locally is only ever checked locally, so a directory account of the same name cannot be reached through it.

Not here: a password reset by e-mail, a forced change at first sign-in, a second factor, and row rules per user (use a key, the directory or the identity provider for those).

docs.title: Signing in with a directory (lldap, OpenLDAP, Active Directory)
docs.text:
For a company that has a directory and no identity provider, truejoin can check a username and password against it. Nothing is stored in truejoin: the directory says who the person is and which groups they belong to, and the configuration says what each group may do.

settings:
  auth:
    enabled: true
    ldap:
      preset: lldap                    # lldap | openldap | active_directory | freeipa
      url: ldaps://ldap.example.com:636   # or ldap:// with start_tls: true
      bind_dn: uid=truejoin,ou=people,dc=example,dc=com   # a read-only search account
      bind_password: ${file:/run/secrets/ldap_bind}
      user_base: ou=people,dc=example,dc=com
      allowed_groups: [analysts, stewards]   # empty = anyone the directory finds
      group_roles:                           # group -> roles (an unmapped group is a role of its own name)
        analysts: [analyst]
        stewards: [steward]
      role_permissions:                      # as for API keys and auth.oidc
        analyst: [read, query]
        steward: [read, query, update, create]
      session_ttl_seconds: 28800             # how long a sign-in lasts

A preset fills the user filter and attributes for that product (lldap and Active Directory read the groups from the user's own memberOf; OpenLDAP searches group_base for groups listing the user). Anything the file writes wins. For another directory, set user_filter (with {username}), username_attr, and either member_of_attr or group_base and group_filter (with {user_dn}).

How a sign-in goes: the username is escaped into the search filter, a service account finds exactly one entry, and the password is checked by binding as that entry. An empty password is refused before any bind (many servers treat it as an anonymous bind and answer success). A wrong password and an unknown user get the same answer. After max_failures wrong passwords (5) a username is paused for lockout_seconds (300) with 429 and Retry-After; one address may fail ten times as often before it is paused, so an office behind one proxy is not locked out by one person's typing.

What the person receives is a token signed by truejoin (HS256, keyed from TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY), good for session_ttl_seconds. It is a bearer token like an identity provider's, so the console, scripts and MCP clients need nothing else:

curl -s -X POST https://truejoin.example.com/ui/sign-in/password \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"username": "ayse", "password": "..."}'
# {"access_token": "...", "expires_at": 1795000000, "name": "Ayşe Yılmaz"}

The token carries the person and their roles, not their permissions: what a role may do is read from the configuration when the token is used, so narrowing a role applies to people already signed in. There is no refresh token: when the sign-in ends the next call answers 401 and the person signs in again. The console shows Sign in with a password when auth.ldap or auth.users is set (beside Sign in, if auth.oidc is too).

In production, truejoin refuses ldap:// without start_tls, a missing TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY (sessions would end at every restart and workers could not accept each other's), and auth.ldap with auth.enabled: false. tls_ca_file names a CA bundle for a private certificate; certificates are always checked.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Every analytical tool call (REST /olap/tools, MCP, the console) also leaves a tool_call event in the audit trail: who, which tool, how it went (answered, empty, refused, failed, error), how long it took and how many rows came back, and how the request was read, by name only: the table, the measures, the breakdowns, the columns a condition was on and the abbreviations the glossary wrote out. Never a value, never the SQL: a condition on status = 'iptal' is recorded as durum.

The words of a question asked in words are not kept unless audit.question_text: true, because a question can name a person ("how much did Ayşe Yılmaz spend"). With them, the console's Usage reading (Administration, Audit; audit permission) lists the questions that met no rows or a refusal, which is where the glossary and the terms fall short; without them it shows how those calls were read.

With the words kept, the summary also reads every question as check_question would and lists the words the vocabulary does not know: each with how many distinct questions used it, how many calls, how many of those were not answered, and one question it came in. The ones in unanswered questions come first, then the most asked. A question answered with a word skipped still counts as answered, so a word can top this list while every call says answered: that is the reading quietly leaving it out. The words are read as the person looking at the summary, so a value hidden from them by a mask shows as a gap. This is what to teach the vocabulary next (a synonym, a value, a glossary entry), from real questions rather than a benchmark. It is under vocabulary in GET /audit/usage, and absent when no words are kept.

A key that may also edit catalogs gets a Means field on each word in the console, which says where the word goes:

  • the glossary, written out as other words ("kargo firmasına" → "şube"): PATCH /catalog/{db}/guidance with {"add_to_glossary": {"word": "what it means"}};
  • a term, as another name for it: PATCH /catalog/{db}/terms/{term} with {"add_synonyms": ["word"]} (a draft term takes the word too, and reads it once it is certified);
  • one of a term's columns, as another word for it: the same route with {"add_to_columns": {"column": ["word"]}}.

Each is added to what is there, on the server, so two stewards adding at once lose nothing (glossary, synonyms and columns replace the whole list). Only approved catalogs are offered, and the list is counted again at once. The same field appears on the Query screen, under a question it did not answer and above one it answered in part (the answer's unread words), for each word it did not read; adding one asks the question again. That one needs no kept question text: it is the question just asked.

A question can also be answered without a word the vocabulary knows: a number, a table or a breakdown the reading made no use of. The Query screen lists those above the answer (the answer's unused words) with no field to add them, as adding a word changes nothing there. One whose words name tables no single reading joins is refused, with the table it would have been read from and what that would have left out.

A question none of whose words were read is refused, and so is one whose reading would use none of the words that name a table, column or value (a word can match a column by its stem and still be left out). The Query screen says what the catalogs hold instead of the words alone: the terms questions are read with, the draft terms each catalog still has to certify, and the languages the words are in. A question about a table whose term is a draft is not short of words: the term has to be certified first.

Propose places asks a model where the words belong: POST /catalog/suggest-words with {"words": [...], "lang": "tr"} (update) returns, for each word it could place, the catalog, the term and the column with a reason, and the words it could not place. Nothing is saved: the rows are pointed at the proposals and a person adds them. The model (the light one when settings.llm.non_reasoning is set) is sent the words and the names in the approved catalogs: terms, columns, their synonyms and the terms' descriptions. It is not sent stored values, samples or the question.

For questions in another language, list it in settings.i18n.languages (Settings, Language) and analyze the catalog again: the words of a term are drafted in every language listed. An analysis replaces draft terms and leaves certified ones as they are, so add a language before certifying, or add words to certified terms one by one.

The summary is GET /audit/usage (?days=30 for the last thirty days): every tool call in the current audit file is counted, not the newest page of them. It reads the whole file each time and not the rotated ones; past a few hundred MB, keep the trail elsewhere and count it there.

docs.title: Running a pilot
docs.text: A pilot answers one question: on our own data, with our own questions, does it give right answers, and does it refuse the ones it cannot read? The customer runs it on their own server. Nobody from outside sees the data, and the report that comes out holds counts and verdicts only.

docs.title: What it measures
docs.text:
Each question gets one verdict:

Verdict Means correct The rows are the expected rows (by value and position in the row, not by column name; in any order unless the question asks for one). refused It said it could not read or answer the question. This is not a wrong answer. wrong It answered, and the rows differ from the expected ones. not checked The expected query did not run, or the answer has more rows than a tool returns (100).

The pilot passes when at most two of twenty answers are wrong (--max-wrong). Refusals do not count against it: a refusal is a question the vocabulary does not know yet, which the steward can teach it (see Deployment, the usage summary).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install and connect as in Deployment. olap.terms must be on (the default).

2. Review the catalog and certify its terms. Questions in words are read only through certified terms:

truejoin catalog -c config/database.yaml analyze -d banka
truejoin catalog -c config/database.yaml review  -d banka
truejoin catalog -c config/database.yaml approve -d banka --certify-terms

Check the labels the review gave the personal columns (email, name, phone, national_id, tc_no): the masks key on them.

3. Make a pilot key with the masks and row rules a real user would have. The pilot then sees what that user sees, and so does its expected answer:

settings:
  auth:
    enabled: true
    api_keys:
      - key: ${file:/run/secrets/truejoin/pilot-key}
        name: pilot
        permissions: [query]
        # row_filters: {musteriler: [{column: sube_kodu, value: IST01}]}
  masking:
    enabled: true
    rules: {email: redact, name: partial, phone: last4, national_id: last4, tc_no: last4}

4. Write the questions. Twenty questions people in the company really ask, each with the right answer, in a file like examples/pilot/questions.yaml in the repository. Write the expected answers before the first run, and do not change them after.

5. Run it:

truejoin pilot run questions.yaml -c config/database.yaml --as pilot --out pilot-report.md

It prints … correct, … refused, … wrong, … not checked and writes the report: wrong answers first, then refusals, then the rest. Every question runs through the same path any caller's does, so each is in the audit trail.

6. Send the report. pilot-report.md names the questions by id only and holds no row values and no SQL, so it can leave the company. For your own reading, --with-questions adds the question text and the refusal messages; that copy stays inside.

docs.title: Showing two users the same question
docs.text:
truejoin pilot compare "Şube bazında toplam işlem tutarı" -c config/database.yaml --as manager --as branch_ist

asks one question as each key and prints the answers one after the other: the rows each one gets under its own row rules and masks. This output does hold row values; it is for a screen in the room, not for sending.

docs.title: Measures from the query history
docs.text:
truejoin catalog suggest reads what a database has been asked before and offers the expressions its queries repeat as draft measures. A draft is read by nothing until someone certifies it.

truejoin catalog suggest -d sales            # mine, name, store as drafts
truejoin catalog certify -d sales -e paid_total -e net_amount

A certified expression is a measure at once: a running server picks the change up within 30 seconds.

suggest needs a catalog whose tables have terms (truejoin catalog analyze with olap.terms on). It reads two things and uses whichever it may:

  • the statement history: the most-run SELECT statements;
  • the view definitions of the configured schema.

From each statement it takes what sits inside an aggregate (SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN total END)), arithmetic that is selected (total - discount AS net) and each condition of a WHERE, as a 1/0 flag to be summed. An expression is kept only when all of its columns belong to one table of the catalog and it holds no parameter, subquery, aggregate or window. A condition or arithmetic on a key or on a date is dropped: id = 7 and created_at >= '2024-01-01' say which rows one query wanted, not what something is. What a view defines is ranked first; the rest by how often it ran. The model then names the candidates and may drop some. It never writes or changes an expression.

docs.title: What each engine needs
docs.text:
Engine Statement history Grant Views PostgreSQL pg_stat_statements the extension in shared_preload_libraries, CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements, and GRANT pg_read_all_stats to see other users' statements information_schema.views (views the user owns or is a member of the owner of) SQL Server sys.dm_exec_query_stats GRANT VIEW SERVER STATE (VIEW DATABASE STATE on Azure SQL) sys.sql_modules, with VIEW DEFINITION Oracle V$SQL GRANT SELECT ON V_$SQL TO <user>, given by SYS in the pluggable database (SYSTEM cannot) ALL_VIEWS MySQL / MariaDB performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest GRANT SELECT ON performance_schema.* TO <user>; on MariaDB also performance_schema=ON (off by default) information_schema.VIEWS

Without the grant suggest says what is missing and carries on with the views. With neither readable it exits with an error.

Four things to know before relying on it:

  • PostgreSQL stores statements with their constants replaced by $1. A condition such as status = 'paid' arrives as status = $1 and is not mined. Arithmetic without a constant survives. On PostgreSQL the views are where the definitions with literals are.
  • MySQL 8 keeps one real statement per digest (QUERY_SAMPLE_TEXT), literals included, cut at performance_schema_max_sql_text_length (1024 by default; a cut statement does not parse and is skipped). MariaDB has only the digest, constants replaced by ? as on PostgreSQL. Either way it reaches back to the server's last restart.
  • SQL Server and Oracle keep the statement as it was written, literals included, so conditions are mined from their history as well. What they keep is the plan cache and the shared pool: it reaches back to the last restart or flush.
  • Oracle's AWR (DBA_HIST_SQLTEXT) is not queried. It reaches further back, and reading it needs the Diagnostics Pack licence.

All the readers are run against real servers by the integration suite (tests/warp/integration/test_query_history.py): PostgreSQL with and without the extension, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server and Oracle.

docs.title: Writing a measure by hand
docs.text:
A reviewer can write one too, on a term in the console's catalog review (Add a measure) or through the API:

curl -X POST "$TRUEJOIN/api/v1/catalog/sales/terms/order/measures/check" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"table": "orders", "expression": "total - discount"}'
curl -X POST "$TRUEJOIN/api/v1/catalog/sales/terms/order/measures" \
  -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"table": "orders", "name": "net_amount", "expression": "total - discount",
       "description": "What the customer paid"}'

The expression is what goes inside the aggregate, written in DuckDB SQL over the table's columns: total - discount, not SUM(total - discount). It is held to the rules a mined expression follows (one table of the term, no subquery, aggregate, window or parameter), then summed over an empty table of those columns in an in-memory DuckDB, where measures run: text multiplied by a number, or a sum of text, is refused there with the engine's reason rather than on the first question that uses it. check stores nothing.

What is added is a draft, exactly like a suggestion, and becomes a measure when it is certified. DELETE .../measures/{name} removes a draft or a measure; a certified one stops being offered at once. Both are audited by name, never by their SQL, which may hold literals.

docs.title: What a reviewer certifies
docs.text:
Business terms: what people call a table, its columns and the values they hold.

A term is written by a model once per table and then reviewed, like the rest of the catalog. Until someone certifies it, nothing reads it: the semantic model, the question planner and the published context all take certified terms of an approved catalog and nothing else.

The proof gate: a repaired statement differs from the original by one literal.

When a condition compares a column with a value it does not hold ('Premium' where the data says 'premium'), the fix is to swap that one string. Whoever proposes the fix, a rewriter here or a model elsewhere, is not trusted to have changed only that: the candidate runs only if this proves it. After the literal-repair gate in NVIDIA Auto Ontology.

Parser-free, like the rest of sql_text: the check must not depend on a candidate being something a particular parser round-trips.
