Bases: BaseModel

A measure that is an expression over one table's columns.

Certified separately from its term: an expression decides what a number means, which is a bigger claim than a synonym.

docs.title: Term
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

One business concept: a name, the words for it, and where it lives.

docs.title: attribute(table, column)
docs.text: The words for table.column, if the term has any.

docs.title: certified_sql(table)
docs.text: The expressions on table a reviewer signed off.

docs.title: carry_over(fresh, previous, columns)
docs.text:
fresh terms, with the certified ones of an earlier catalog kept as they were.

A certified term is a reviewer's work, and re-analysing the database must not replace it with a new guess. It is kept when every table it covers is still there, minus the columns that are not. columns maps each table of the new catalog to its column names.

docs.title: clean_words(words, *avoid)
docs.text:
Words as a model or a person wrote them, made usable.

Not a list becomes none; blanks, repeats and the name itself are dropped.

docs.title: prove_substitution(original_sql, candidate_sql, absent, present, validate)
docs.text:
Whether candidate_sql is original_sql with absent replaced by present.

True only when all of these hold: the original had the literal absent; the candidate has present everywhere the original had absent and is otherwise the same literals in the same order; with literals blanked the two statements are identical; and validate (the guardrails every query passes) accepts the candidate. Only string literals are covered.

docs.title: split_literals(sql)
docs.text:
sql with every string literal blanked, and the literals in order.

Quoted identifiers stay in the skeleton: a candidate that renamed a column is not the same statement.

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records
docs.text:
These ADRs capture significant architectural and process decisions, following the lightweight format popularized by Michael Nygard.

# Title Status 0001 Layered architecture enforced by import-linter Superseded by 0007 0002 Fail-safe production configuration validation Accepted 0003 Dependency management: ranges + hashed lockfile Accepted 0004 LLM sample-data privacy (cloud opt-in + PII masking) Accepted 0005 CI quality gates: pragmatic, then strict Accepted 0006 Distribution name vs. the import package Superseded by 0010 0007 Hexagonal architecture (ports & adapters) Accepted 0008 Dialect abstraction and the ODBC (SQL Server) adapter Accepted 0009 Row security, column masking and the audit trail Accepted 0010 One package, one process Accepted 0011 The sync/async bridge: one loop thread owns the OLAP side's gateways Accepted 0012 Row rules and masks on analytical queries, by rewriting the query Accepted 0013 Nothing a model wrote is read until a reviewer certifies it Accepted

docs.title: 1. Layered architecture enforced by import-linter
docs.text:
• Status: Superseded by ADR-0007
  • Date: 2026-06-23

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The codebase grew organically and had at least one circular dependency (llm ↔ enrichment). Without an enforced dependency direction, low-level modules risk importing high-level ones, making the system hard to reason about, test, and reuse.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Define explicit layers and enforce their dependency direction with import-linter contracts in pyproject.toml ([tool.importlinter]), run as a blocking CI gate (lint-imports):

  • core and config are the lowest layers and import nothing else in warp.
  • database imports no app/domain modules.
  • catalog must not depend on llm, enrichment, api, or integration.
  • schema and utils must not depend on api or integration.

The llm ↔ enrichment runtime cycle was broken by importing TableSamples under TYPE_CHECKING in llm/prompts.py.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Dependency direction is verifiable and regressions are caught in CI.
  • New code must respect the contracts (see CONTRIBUTING).
  • A few contracts are intentionally conservative; they can be tightened (e.g. a strict total ordering) as the architecture stabilizes.

docs.title: 2. Fail-safe production configuration validation
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-06-23

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The defaults convenient for development (auth disabled, raw SQL endpoint on, CORS_ORIGINS=*, docs exposed) are dangerous in production. Relying on operators to remember to flip every switch is error-prone and fails silently.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Add validate_production_config() (in warp.config.settings), called during app startup. When APP_ENV=production, it raises ConfigurationError and refuses to start if any unsafe condition holds:

  • auth.enabled is false
  • settings.enable_raw_query is true
  • CORS_ORIGINS contains *

These options keep their developer-friendly defaults outside production. The shipped image defaults to APP_ENV=production, so a misconfigured deployment fails loudly at boot.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Insecure production deployments fail fast and visibly instead of silently exposing the API.
  • Operators must provide explicit, safe values (documented in docs/docs/deployment.md and .env.example).
  • The check is centralized and unit-tested.

docs.title: Addendum (1.0.0)
docs.text: The check now lives in truejoin.application.settings.validate_production_config, and ConfigurationError in truejoin.domain.gateway.errors. It also covers the settings added since: auth.oidc, auth.ldap (no plain ldap://, a TRUEJOIN_SECRET_KEY for sessions) and auth.users.

docs.title: 3. Dependency management: ranges + hashed lockfile
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-06-23

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The project is consumed both as a library (pip install) and deployed as an application (Docker). Libraries want flexible version ranges to avoid conflicts for downstream consumers; deployments want exact, reproducible, verifiable dependencies.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Keep flexible lower-bound ranges (>=) in pyproject.toml for library consumers.
  • Generate two universal, hashed lock files with make lock: requirements.lock (all extras; CI and local development) and requirements-prod.lock (runtime + llm + odbc; the Docker image).
  • Install from the locks with --require-hashes (uv pip sync) in CI and in the Dockerfile builder stage; never resolve from ranges in a deployment.
  • Migrated the Gemini provider off the EOL google-generativeai SDK to google-genai.
  • Dependabot keeps both Python deps and the SHA-pinned GitHub Actions current.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Library consumers retain resolution flexibility; deployments are deterministic and tamper-evident (hashes).
  • Both lock files must be regenerated (make lock) whenever pyproject.toml dependencies change; CI installs from them, so a stale lock fails fast.

docs.title: Addendum (1.0.0)
docs.text: The two hashed lock files became one uv.lock (ADR-0010): make lock runs uv lock, and CI and the Dockerfile install with uv sync --frozen, which checks every hash. Dependabot is not configured in this repository.

docs.title: 4. LLM sample-data privacy (cloud opt-in + PII masking)
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-06-23

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Catalog intelligence sends table samples to an LLM to generate descriptions. Sample rows can contain personal or sensitive data. Sending that to a third-party (cloud) LLM provider is a privacy risk that should never happen implicitly.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
In warp.enrichment.analyzer, gate sample data before it reaches the prompt:

  • Cloud opt-in: cloud providers (openai, anthropic, gemini) receive no raw samples unless analysis.share_samples_with_cloud_llm is enabled. Local providers (Ollama) are exempt.
  • PII masking: when analysis.mask_pii_samples is enabled (default), values of columns whose names match PII patterns (email, phone, ssn, password, token, …) are masked to *** before any LLM call.

The unmodified samples are still used to populate the catalog locally.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No sensitive sample data leaves the machine to a cloud LLM by default.
  • Pattern-based PII detection is heuristic (name-based); operators can extend analysis.pii_column_patterns. Semantic-type-based masking is a possible future enhancement once a catalog already exists.

docs.title: Addendum (0.9.0): storage-time masking and OpenAPI examples
docs.text: Masking the LLM prompt was not enough: the stored catalog was re-published through the draft API and injected into /openapi.json as example values. Sample values of PII columns — matched by analysis.pii_column_patterns on the name or by the LLM's semantic_type (email, phone, name, address) — are therefore dropped before a ColumnCatalogEntry is built (warp.domain.samples.samples_for_storage). Writing examples into the OpenAPI spec is a separate opt-in, catalog.openapi_include_examples (default false), and the spec route itself is protected by the auth manager (see the security policy).

docs.title: Addendum (1.0.0)
docs.text: The analyzer is now truejoin/application/catalog/catalog_analysis.py, and samples_for_storage is truejoin.domain.gateway.samples.samples_for_storage.

docs.title: 5. CI quality gates: pragmatic, then strict
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-06-23

docs.title: Context
docs.text: When CI was introduced, the codebase did not yet pass its own intended gates: ~597 ruff errors, 147 mypy --strict errors, ~49% coverage, and 4 broken tests. Making every gate blocking immediately would have left CI red and blocked all work; making none blocking would let quality keep drifting.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Introduce CI green from day one, then ratchet each gate to blocking as the debt was cleared:

  1. Start: pytest blocking; ruff / mypy / coverage non-blocking (reported).
  2. Clear the backlog incrementally — fix the broken tests, clean ruff to zero, fix all mypy --strict errors, raise coverage to ≥80%.
  3. Flip each gate to blocking once it passes.

End state — all blocking and green: pytest, coverage ≥80%, ruff, mypy --strict, lint-imports. pip-audit runs advisory (non-blocking) to avoid surprise breakage from new advisories. Actions are SHA-pinned with least-privilege permissions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• CI was useful immediately and never blocked progress on pre-existing debt.
  • Quality cannot regress below the current bar.
  • Adding new rule sets (e.g. ruff D/PL/C901) is deferred — they would add ~789 errors (mostly docstrings) and belong to a dedicated pass.

docs.title: Addendum (1.0.0)
docs.text: import-linter and lint-imports were replaced by one dependency walker, tests/fusion/architecture/test_dependency_rules.py (ADR-0010), which runs with the tests. mypy is strict on truejoin.domain, truejoin.ports and truejoin.application only ([[tool.mypy.overrides]] in pyproject.toml); CI runs uv run mypy truejoin.

docs.title: 6. Distribution name vs. the import package
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted (applied in 0.9.0); superseded by ADR-0010 in 1.0.0, where the distribution and the import package are both truejoin
  • Date: 2026-06-23

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project is named Warp, which collides with several well-known projects:

  • NVIDIA Warp (warp-lang on PyPI) — a Python framework for GPU simulation.
  • Warp (warpdotdev) — a popular terminal.
  • Other smaller uses of "warp" across ecosystems.

The PyPI distribution name warp is effectively unavailable / ambiguous, and the name is hard to discover and search for.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
If/when publishing to PyPI, use a namespaced distribution name while keeping the import package as warp:

  • distribution name: e.g. warp-engine (or warp-crud, warp-api)
  • import name: warp (unchanged) — pip install warp-engine then import warp

This is a metadata-only change ([project] name in pyproject.toml) and does not affect source code. Re-evaluate the import name only if it proves confusing.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Avoids a name clash on PyPI and improves discoverability.
  • Project marketing/name ("Warp Engine") stays intact.
  • Deferred until publication; tracked here so it is not forgotten.

docs.title: 7. Hexagonal architecture (ports & adapters)
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-09-17
  • Supersedes: ADR-0001

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The layered contracts of ADR-0001 kept packages from importing "upwards", but they could not express the properties that actually matter for this code base: the domain must not know FastAPI or asyncpg; the analysis use case must not construct database readers, an LLM client and a file store itself; and the wiring must exist in exactly one place. In practice composition was duplicated across main.py, cli.py and integration/pipeline.py (with a bug in two of them), the catalog file store mixed persistence with the review workflow, an HTTP handler built the whole enrichment pipeline inline, and module-level singletons (AppState, _settings, _auth_manager) made the app hard to test.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Four layers with a strict inward dependency direction, enforced by import-linter ([tool.importlinter] in pyproject.toml):

Layer Package Rules Entry points warp.main, warp.cli may import anything; own the process (uvicorn, console script) Composition root warp.infrastructure builds outbound adapters and the Container; loads config; sets up logging Adapters warp.adapters.inbound.{http,cli}, warp.adapters.outbound.{db,llm,catalog_store,export} may import application and domain only; inbound and outbound are independent of each other, as are http and cli Application warp.application use-case services, ports (typing.Protocol), configuration models, the Container type; imports domain only; no frameworks/drivers Domain warp.domain entities and pure rules (stdlib + pydantic); imports nothing else

Key mechanics:

  • Ports (warp.application.ports): DatabaseGateway/SqlReader/ DatabaseGatewayFactory, CommentSource/SampleSource, CatalogRepository, TextGenerator, CatalogExporter. Adapters satisfy them structurally; tests substitute fakes without patching.
  • Composition root: infrastructure.bootstrap.build_container(settings, *, repository=, gateway_factory=, text_generator_factory=, analysis_factory=) returns an application.container.Container. The HTTP app takes a container factory (create_app(container_factory, env)), the CLI group receives one through context_settings["obj"]; neither adapter imports infrastructure.
  • Runtime state lives on app.state.runtime (RuntimeContext) and in RuntimeEnv, not in module globals.
  • Review workflow transitions are pure functions in domain.catalog_review; CatalogReviewService applies them over the repository; CatalogFileStore only persists.
  • No compatibility shims: 0.9.0 changes import paths outright.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Import paths changed (breaking); the test tree mirrors the layers.
  • Any adapter can be swapped in tests or by embedders (in-memory repository, fake gateway, recorded LLM) by passing it to build_container.
  • The full startup sequence is exercised in tests over a fake gateway.
  • Adding a database or LLM provider means adding an outbound adapter that satisfies the port; no application code changes.

docs.title: Addendum (1.0.0)
docs.text: These packages now live under truejoin.* (ADR-0010): warp.main → truejoin.main, warp.cli → truejoin.adapters.inbound.cli.main, warp.infrastructure and its bootstrap.build_container → truejoin.bootstrap.build_container, warp.adapters.* → truejoin.adapters.*, warp.application.ports → the flat truejoin.ports, and domain.catalog_review → truejoin.domain.catalog.catalog_review. RuntimeEnv is in truejoin.application.settings. The import-linter contracts mentioned above were replaced by tests/fusion/architecture/test_dependency_rules.py.

docs.title: 8. Dialect abstraction and the ODBC (SQL Server) adapter
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-09-17

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Warp supported PostgreSQL (asyncpg) and MySQL (aiomysql). Everything that differs between the two — placeholder style ($1 vs %s), identifier quoting, ILIKE vs LIKE, RETURNING, LIMIT/OFFSET, the default schema and the catalog queries for comments and row counts — was expressed as if dialect == "postgresql" branches spread over six modules. Adding a third engine meant touching all of them.

SQL Server was the requested third engine. There is no maintained native asyncio driver for it; the standard route is ODBC (pyodbc, wrapped for asyncio by aioodbc) with Microsoft's msodbcsql18 driver. ODBC also opens the door to other data sources (Oracle, DB2, …) through the same code path.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. One Dialect object per engine (adapters/outbound/db/dialect.py), a frozen dataclass holding the placeholder style, quote characters, LIKE operator, how written rows are returned (returning / output / refetch), pagination style (LIMIT/OFFSET or OFFSET … FETCH), percent escaping, default schema and the comment / row-count catalog queries. The query builder, the named-parameter binder, identifier quoting, the metadata readers and the composition root consume the Dialect; none of them branch on a database-type string any more. PostgreSQL and MySQL SQL is unchanged byte for byte.
  2. A single ODBCAdapter with two profiles selected by the config type:
  3. mssql / sqlserver — first-class: introspection through INFORMATION_SCHEMA and sys.* (identity/computed markers, keys, indexes), writes that return the row with OUTPUT (falling back per table to SCOPE_IDENTITY() + re-select when triggers make OUTPUT illegal, error 334), TOP/OFFSET … FETCH, a datetimeoffset output converter, comments from MS_Description extended properties and row counts from sys.partitions. Covered by real-database integration tests in CI.
  4. odbc — best effort: ANSI quoting, ? placeholders, introspection via the ODBC catalog functions, re-select after writes, no catalog intelligence. Unit-tested only; documented as such.
  5. Packaging: aioodbc lives in an odbc extra and is imported lazily in connect(), so the factory and the unit tests run without it. The ODBC driver is a system package: the Docker image installs msodbcsql18 by default (--build-arg WITH_MSSQL_ODBC=0 opts out), CI installs it on the Ubuntu runner, developers install it locally (brew install msodbcsql18 / apt). The lock (now the one uv.lock, ADR-0003 addendum) includes aioodbc/pyodbc.
  6. Tests: SQL Server integration tests run in CI (WARP_REQUIRE_MSSQL=1 turns "unavailable" into a failure) and auto-skip on machines without the driver or without an x86-64 Docker engine (the SQL Server image has no arm64 build). WARP_MSSQL_HOST points them at an existing server instead.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Adding an engine is now one Dialect entry plus, when the driver's execution model differs, one adapter; the SQL helpers need no changes.
  • Oracle (added later) proved the claim, and found three gaps in it. The first Dialect split engine differences along axes that happened to coincide for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server, so three of them had to become fields of their own before a fourth engine fitted: sample_style (Oracle paginates with OFFSET ... FETCH like SQL Server but has no SELECT TOP (n)), unsorted_pagination_filler (Oracle needs no ORDER BY before the row-limiting clause, and rejects SQL Server's ORDER BY (SELECT NULL) because a SELECT without FROM is invalid), and identifier_case (Oracle folds unquoted identifiers to upper case, so quoting users does not find a table stored as USERS). Adding Oracle itself was then one Dialect entry, one introspection profile on the existing ODBCAdapter, and its integration tests.
  • ColumnSchema.is_auto_generated gives create models and required-column checks one definition of "the database fills this in" (auto-increment, serial, identity, computed). PostgreSQL identity columns are now recognised too.
  • SQL Server identifiers are bracket-quoted through the same strict sanitizer, so the identifier-injection guarantees are unchanged.
  • The generic profile cannot detect identity columns unless the driver reports them in TYPE_NAME, and DELETE costs an extra SELECT because rowcounts may be unreported; both are acceptable for a best-effort path.
  • aioodbc 0.5's statistics() wrapper drops pyodbc's mandatory table argument; the adapter works around it and degrades to "no index metadata" rather than failing.

docs.title: 9. Row security, column masking and the audit trail
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-09-19

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Warp turns a database into an API with very little configuration, which is the point — and the risk. The three questions an operator in a regulated setting (KVKK, BDDK) has to answer about such an API are:

  1. Can a caller read rows that are not theirs?
  2. Can a caller read column values they should not see?
  3. Can anyone show, afterwards, what a given caller actually saw?

Before this change the answers were "yes", "yes" and "no". Permissions existed, but only as coarse verbs (read, create, …) with no notion of which rows or which columns, and nothing was recorded beyond ordinary request logs.

An adjacent constraint shaped the design: the identity built during authentication never reached a route. Every router registers auth as dependencies=[Depends(auth.require(...))], and FastAPI discards what such a dependency returns, so the AuthenticatedUser was constructed and thrown away.

docs.title: Identity reaches the handler
docs.text: permission_checker records the caller on request.state before returning it, and caller_of / policy_of / roles_of read it back. Nothing else changes — no route signature had to move. None means "nobody was identified" (auth off, or a public path) and is never treated as "permitted".

docs.title: Row-level security is a filter, not a check
docs.text:
An API key carries tenant, roles and per-table row_filters, written in the same vocabulary as user filters so they can simply be ANDed onto a query. Two enforcement paths, because there are two kinds of access:

  • Reads with a WHERE clause (list, count, export, stream) push the conditions into SQL. The database never returns a row the caller may not see, and the caller's own filters can only narrow further — policy conditions are appended last.
  • Reads and writes addressed by primary key have no WHERE to push into, so the row is fetched and matched in memory. A row outside the policy is reported as 404, not 403: telling a caller that a record exists but is not theirs is itself a disclosure.

Writes are checked in both directions. A caller cannot create a row into a scope they cannot read, cannot move a row there with an update, and cannot omit the scope column and let a database default decide it.

Raw SQL is denied to any key with row rules, even one holding all. Conditions cannot be pushed into a statement the caller wrote, and one SELECT would make the rules irrelevant.

docs.title: Masking is keyed on meaning, not on names
docs.text:
Masking rules attach to the catalog's semantic types (email, phone, address, …), not to column names. This is the whole reason the LLM catalog earns its place here: when it labels a newly discovered contact_email, that column is masked from that moment, rather than leaking until somebody remembers to write a rule for it.

Only an approved catalog is used. A draft's labels have not been reviewed, and masking the wrong columns is as damaging as masking none.

A mask must produce a value the response can still carry, so the text strategies require a text column and null requires a nullable one. Anything that does not fit is reported at startup, naming the column, rather than failing response validation on the first row that reaches it.

docs.title: hash is a pseudonym, and it is keyed
docs.text:
Four of the five strategies destroy the value. hash does not: it exists because none of the others preserves equality across rows, and a masked column that can still be joined on is a real analytics capability. The output is therefore a pseudonym, and the word matters — under KVKK a pseudonym is still personal data, so an export of hash-masked rows has not been anonymised and cannot be treated as if it had.

It is keyed for a reason that is not a matter of taste. An unkeyed digest of enumerable data is not a mask: an email address falls to a wordlist, and a TCKN is eleven digits with a check rule, so the valid space is about a billion and a laptop walks all of it. Widening the digest does nothing about that — the attack is enumeration, not collision. The key is what moves the attack from "anyone holding the exported file" to "anyone holding the key", which is the standard pseudonymisation posture: keep the key apart from the data.

Two consequences an operator has to accept. Rotating or losing the key breaks correlation with anything exported earlier — that is the cost of stability, and it is the right trade, because a key that changed per process would make the strategy useless for the one thing it is for. And a hash rule with no key refuses startup. The two tempting alternatives are both worse: skipping the rule leaves a PII column unmasked while the configuration says otherwise, and falling back to an unkeyed digest reintroduces the defect under a name that sounds safe. A masking layer must not return a readable value while reporting that it masked it.

docs.title: The audit trail records restriction, not data
docs.text:
One event per data-touching request: who, when, which database and table, which action, how many rows, the request id — and, crucially, whether a row filter applied and which columns were masked. An audit log that cannot distinguish "read the table" from "read their own tenant, with the email column masked" cannot answer the only question it is ever asked.

What an event never carries is the data: no row values, no filter literals, no SQL parameters. Filter column names are recorded; the values compared against them are not. An audit trail that quotes the data it audits becomes a second copy of that data, in a file with weaker access controls and longer retention than the database it came from.

A change to a catalog is audited the same way, as a catalog_change event: the catalog decides what is masked and what a question means, so who approved a table or certified a measure matters as much as who read one. It names what changed (fields, columns, terms, measures) and never the text written or an expression's SQL, which may hold literals.

Sinks must never raise. An audit sink that can fail a request turns a logging problem into an outage.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Masking configured with a hash rule and no masking.hash_secret is refused by MaskingConfig itself, so it fails where the configuration is read rather than where masking is applied. That matters because the application point sits behind auto_discover_tables: validating there would have made the refusal depend on an unrelated feature flag and on the environment. Production additionally refuses a secret short enough to be guessed, which is a question about strength rather than presence.
  • Row rules mean nothing without authentication, so auth.enabled: false with row_filters configured refuses startup in production. The same hazard exists for a data path listed in auth.public_paths, which the README warns about but cannot detect generically.
  • The CRUDOperations instance is shared across requests, so the policy is bound per request through with_policy rather than stored on the instance — a cached instance carrying one tenant's rules is precisely the bug this feature exists to prevent.
  • Masking and auditing travel together as a Governance bundle: every route that withholds something should also record that it did.
  • The audit sink is built in the composition root and reaches the HTTP layer through the Container, because an inbound adapter may not import an outbound one (ADR-0007).
  • Writing this exposed a gap in the test harness: MockDatabaseAdapter.select ignored its filters argument, so every route test that exercised filter[column][op] only proved the request did not error. It now filters as SQL would — which is what lets a test notice a missing condition.

docs.title: 10. One package, one process
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Warp, Fusion and Stargate were three repositories and, deployed together, three processes: Fusion read the database through Warp over HTTP, and an MCP server generated by Stargate would have called Warp over HTTP again. For an on-premises customer that is three things to install, three configurations that have to agree, and two network hops inside one product. It also put the governance in the wrong place: Warp enforced row rules and masks on its table routes, and Fusion, which runs arbitrary SQL over the same data, knew nothing of them.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
One distribution (truejoin), one import package, one hexagonal tree. The three histories were imported with git filter-repo into subdirectories and then moved, so git log --follow and blame still work.

Inside each layer the origins stay recognisable (domain/olap, domain/gateway, domain/governance, domain/catalog, domain/mcp), ports are one flat package, and one dependency walker replaces three mechanisms. The one exception to "the domain imports nothing" is pydantic, for the catalog's file format.

One process serves the REST gateway, /olap and MCP on one port, behind one set of API keys. The OLAP side reads the databases through the gateway's own DatabaseGateway port, in process. The HTTP source survives as warp-remote, for a gateway on another node.

The MCP server is curated, not generated. Generating tools from the gateway's OpenAPI gives five write tools per table, the opposite of a read-only analyst surface. The product's MCP server exposes the analytical tools by profile (analyst, admin) and allow-list; Stargate remains as a library and truejoin mcp convert for turning any OpenAPI or Postman spec into an MCP server.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One config file, one CLI, one image. The pre-1.0 FUSION_* and WARP_* variables are still applied on top of the file, and logged as deprecated.
  • The OLAP side needs its own database pools (see ADR 11), so each database has two.
  • A process holds what it loaded: one replica per deployment. Scaling out means a gateway on another node and warp-remote.
  • trio was a placeholder name; renaming it to truejoin (2026-11-13) was one mechanical commit.

docs.title: 11. The sync/async bridge: one loop thread owns the OLAP side's gateways
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The gateway is async: asyncpg, aiomysql and aioodbc pools belong to the event loop that created them. The OLAP engine is synchronous: DuckDB behind one lock, services written as plain functions, about nine hundred tests that call them directly. Once the engine reads databases in process instead of over HTTP, the two have to meet.

Three kinds of caller reach the engine: REST handlers (run by the server in a thread pool), MCP tool calls (run by the MCP library in a worker thread) and the CLI. None of them is on the loop that owns a pool.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GatewayLoop is a daemon thread running its own event loop. The OLAP side's gateways are created and connected on it and never leave it. submit(coro, timeout) schedules a coroutine there and waits for the result.

InProcessSource implements the engine's DataSource port on top: schema discovery, row estimates and slice reads become submit calls. A slice is streamed: a task on the loop thread feeds a bounded queue, and the engine reads batches from it, so a slow consumer slows the database read instead of filling memory.

The engine stays synchronous. Making DataSource async would have changed every service, the store's lock discipline and the test suite, to gain nothing: DuckDB does the work under a lock either way.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Each database has a second pool, for the OLAP side, using the read-only credentials when the database has them.
  • The one way to deadlock is calling submit from the loop thread itself, so that raises immediately.
  • About fifty microseconds per batch for the thread hop.
  • Loads are serialised per source table: two requests that both need a table not loaded yet used to stream into the same staging table. A test with thirty-two concurrent callers found it.

docs.title: 12. Row rules and masks on analytical queries, by rewriting the query
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text: ADR 9 put row rules and column masks on the table routes, where each request reads one table and the gateway builds the SQL. An analytical query is the caller's own SQL over data that is already loaded into DuckDB, whole rows and raw values, for every caller at once. Applying the rules to the result is too late: an aggregate over rows the caller may not see, or a masked column read through an alias, a join or a subquery, has already leaked.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Every analytical read takes an AccessScope: the caller's row policy, the masks that apply to their roles, and who they are. For a restricted scope, each table the query names is replaced by a subquery that carries that caller's row conditions and masks (SqlglotAccessRewriter). Aliases, joins, CTEs, aggregates and subqueries then all read the restricted view, because there is nothing else to read.

Around that:

  • It fails closed. What cannot be wrapped (a materialized view, a slice named directly, a table function, anything that is not a plain source table) refuses the query.
  • Row conditions reach the planner, so a tenant's query on a table too big to load fetches that tenant's slice. A condition or join key on a masked column never narrows a fetch: the query compares the masked value, and fetching by the raw one would let a caller test guesses by counting.
  • No pushdown and no shared cache. The masks are written for the store; the cache key is the rewritten SQL, so two tenants cannot share an entry.
  • Masks come from the approved catalog only, and produce what the table routes produce, the keyed hash included. The result names the columns that show a masked value (masked), traced from the caller's own SQL with sqlglot's lineage (an alias or a CTE keeps the mark; an aggregate drops it). It is a label for the reader: the rewrite does the masking, and the label narrows no fetch.
  • What describes a table says nothing the rows would not. A caller held to row rules on a table is not told its size (list_sources and describe_table answer -1 for row_count and row_estimate), nor shown the slices other callers loaded: the size counts other tenants' rows, and a slice's conditions are their literals.
  • Grounding runs before the rewrite, so a table a repair adds is restricted like the rest.
  • One audit event per read: who, which tables, how many rows, whether row rules applied, which columns were masked. Never the SQL.

query_metrics and answer_question reach the same path. A metric over a masked column is refused rather than computed over masked values.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A restricted caller's queries always run locally, and a query that is not a flat SELECT loads whole tables for them.
  • A new path that returns rows must take the scope or refuse a restricted one; there is no default that leaks.
  • The gateway's raw /query/execute is outside this: it runs on the source database. It refuses callers with row rules or masks, and production refuses to start with it enabled.
  • This is the one component with no precedent in the three origins and it carries the privacy promise. Its tests were written first.

docs.title: 13. Nothing a model wrote is read until a reviewer certifies it
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-05

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A model is good at saying what things are called and bad at being asked on every question: slow, different each time, and able to name what does not exist. NVIDIA's Auto Ontology showed the useful half of this (join-path checks, terms, expressions mined from query history) and left out the other: its certified flag exists in the schema and nothing ever checks it.

Here the stakes are concrete. A relationship decides which joins are accepted. A term decides what a question means. An expression decides what a number is. A semantic type decides which column is masked.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The model works at analysis time, on the schema, and its output is a draft.

What the model writes What makes it count Who reads it then Descriptions, semantic types The table is approved Masking labels, the published context Relationships Approved, and the data bears it out (verified) The join graph Terms: words for tables, columns, values The term is certified Semantic models, answer_question, search_terms Expressions, written or mined The expression is certified, apart from its term Measures

DatabaseCatalog.certified_terms is the one door: an approved catalog and a certified term. Approving a table certifies its term, because the reviewer was just shown it. Approving a whole catalog certifies none; doing that takes --certify-terms, in so many words. What was certified survives re-analysis.

The model can only attach words to names that exist, and can name a mined expression but never write or change one. A certified expression is still held to a shape when it is used: a scalar over its own table's columns.

At query time no model is involved. answer_question matches words against the certified vocabulary, so the same question gets the same answer, and returns the request it understood and the SQL that ran.

The benchmark gate for the term layer was written before its arm existed (bench/README.md). It passed: 37 of 48 against the catalog arm's 34, and nothing invented. The accuracy lead is within noise; what separates the two is that nothing is invented and that joins needing a table in between are right.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A fresh deployment answers questions in words only after a review. Until then answer_question says how to get there, and everything else works.
  • Catalog analysis costs one more model call per table while olap.terms is on.
  • A catalog certified while the server runs goes live at once through the API, or within 30 seconds when certified on the command line.
  • The vocabulary is as good as its coverage: a word nobody certified matches nothing. In the benchmark the deterministic tool alone answers 27 of 48.
